title: Prioritizing Information

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Suppose your backpack is overloaded and you can only carry three things up a hill. Prioritizing is not gathering more items or arranging them neatly, it is judging which three matter most for the trip. Clinical judgment does the same with facts about a person: the facts are already in hand, and the skill is deciding which ones deserve attention first.

### Question 2

A single assessment produces dozens of facts. Any one of them is a cue; a relevant cue is one that actually helps explain what is happening right now. For someone struggling to breathe, the breathing rate is a relevant cue and the person's favorite color is not, even though both are true facts about the same person.

### Question 3

A number carries no meaning until you have something to measure it against. A temperature of 98.9 F tells you nothing on its own; it becomes information once you know the expected range sits near 97 to 99 F. Comparison acts as a filter: values inside the expected range settle into the background, and values outside it get pulled forward for a closer look.

### Question 4

If someone tells you the room smells like smoke and you also see haze near the ceiling, the two clues together are much more convincing than either one alone. One clue arrives through a person's report, the other through your own observation. Skilled thinkers weigh both, and they become most alert when the two independent sources point to the same conclusion.

### Question 5

Picture a stack of blocks. If the bottom block is sliding out, straightening the decorations on top accomplishes nothing, because the whole stack is about to come down. Breathing and circulation are the bottom blocks of a person. Anything threatening them gets attention first, and the higher needs still get attention, just in sequence.

### Question 6

One cloud tells you very little. Clouds thickening and darkening hour after hour tell you a storm is on the way. A single odd measurement may be a fluke of technique or timing, but a value sliding further from normal each time it is checked describes a direction, and direction predicts what happens next.

### Question 7

Highlight every sentence in a textbook and the page turns solid yellow, at which point nothing stands out. Highlighting works only because most of the text stays unmarked. Ranking information uses the same mechanism: deliberately leaving some facts in the background is what allows the critical ones to become visible.

### Question 8

Three of these facts describe how a person lives: when they like dinner, that they use glasses to read, that work is on their mind. The fourth describes a body system running far above its expected pace, since adults usually breathe about 12 to 20 times a minute and this is 30. Breathing cannot be postponed, so that finding moves to the top while the others stay on the list further down.

### Question 9

Individual puzzle pieces show almost nothing, but fit three together and a wheel appears. Dry mouth, low urine output, and thirst are three pieces that fit into one picture of a body running short on fluid. Clustering is the deliberate act of fitting pieces together instead of reading each one in isolation.

### Question 10

A crack in a wall that has looked exactly the same for the past two days is a different problem from a pipe that started leaking this morning. Both are real, but only one is changing. New, plus affecting a function you cannot live without, is the combination that moves a finding to the front of the line.

### Question 11

Cooking follows the same order: look at what is actually in the refrigerator, work out what those ingredients could become, decide which dish is the best use of them, plan it, cook it, then taste it. Deciding on the dish has to come after you know your options and before the stove goes on. Cook first and decide later and dinner is already committed.

### Question 12

Decide in the opening minutes of a mystery who the culprit is, and for the rest of the film you bend each new clue to fit that guess while sliding past the ones that point elsewhere. The same thing happens with an early abnormal finding: it quietly sets the frame for everything after it. That is why experienced clinicians build in the habit of asking what evidence would change their mind.
